areaSummaries.label: backend: auth / RBAC / IDOR / tenant isolation
areaSummaries.summary: The auth/RBAC/tenant-isolation layer is generally well-built: JWT decoding restricts the algorithm (HS256), rejects refresh tokens for access, and enforces token_version revocation; a central require_location_access dependency plus validate_location_access/assert_location_access helpers consistently scope most endpoints to organization_id and per-user UserLocationAccess. The dominant systemic weakness is that require_location_access deliberately enforces ONLY per-user location scope and returns the path location_id unchecked for org-wide roles (Owner/Admin/org-Viewer), relying on each handler to also run an org-filtered query for tenant isolation. That contract is violated in the location health-score endpoint, which queries by raw location_id with no organization_id filter, yielding a cross-tenant IDOR (read + write) for any org admin. A handful of secondary issues: client-supplied storage_key/cdn_url in attach_media let a tenant reference another org's storage object, and several dead/unused security helpers (verify_location_access, check_location_quota) add confusion. No missing auth dependencies were found on the audited routers (auth is per-route, not global, but every data route declares get_current_user/staff_required/etc.).

areaSummaries.label: backend: billing / payments / Razorpay / credits
areaSummaries.summary: The billing area is, on the whole, carefully built: webhook signatures are verified with a constant-time HMAC compare, the webhook idempotency marker (billing_webhook_events.razorpay_event_id, DB-unique) and business writes share one transaction, and every credit/quota grant path re-fetches the org with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which genuinely serializes same-org grants and prevents the classic double-credit. Pricing is server-authoritative and order/subscription ownership is re-validated against notes.organization_id on the reconcile paths, closing the obvious cross-tenant replay. The real risks are subtler: (1) the ledger-row idempotency key razorpay_payment_id has no DB unique constraint, so idempotency depends entirely on the application-level read-then-insert holding under the org row lock — correct today but fragile if any future grant path forgets to lock; (2) AI-credit consumption is deliberately non-atomic (pre-check then post-success deduct on a re-fetch), so concurrent requests can overspend; (3) proration uses integer .days which systematically undercharges by up to a day and zeroes out near cycle end; (4) subscription/add-on refunds only log and never reclaim quota or per-location credits, a money-loss path; (5) several recovery endpoints (locations/unlock, remandate) are excluded from the billing-lock whitelist. No directly exploitable double-charge or cross-tenant leak was found, but the idempotency story relies on an undocumented invariant (always lock the org first) rather than a DB constraint.

areaSummaries.label: backend: celery tasks + beat scheduling
areaSummaries.summary: The Celery layer (backend/app/tasks.py ~3100 lines, backend/app/worker.py) is functional and shows real care around per-task DB sessions, Redis locks, idempotency guards, and error classification for retryable vs permanent failures. However there are several genuine reliability gaps for a thread-pool worker (--pool=threads --concurrency=10): NO global task_time_limit/soft_time_limit and a 1-hour broker visibility_timeout means any long-running task (e.g. reconcile_pending_subscriptions looping synchronous Razorpay calls over all orgs) can be redelivered and run concurrently with itself; acks_late is never set so the whole config relies on app-level locks. The insights orchestrator marks sync_state as completed and evaluates attention flags immediately after only ENQUEUEING per-location tasks (not awaiting them), so flags run on stale data and status is wrong. Several beat fan-out tasks (sync_all_insights_beat_task, retry_failed_sentiment_beat_task, sync_all_active_categories_metadata_task) loop .delay() over every org/location with zero throttling, risking GBP 429 storms and broker floods. sync_insights_task swallows exceptions into a {"status":"failed"} return so failures never retry and never surface as task failures. A scheduled-post code path publishes a non-campaign post to an arbitrary single Location.first() and the whole SCHEDULED-post feature is unreachable (nothing sets that status). Most findings are medium severity; none are clear cross-tenant data leaks (org filtering is consistently present in the task layer).

areaSummaries.label: backend: GBP provider / external API client
areaSummaries.summary: The GBP provider area is functionally rich but has several real correctness and resilience defects. The most serious is an OAuth account-selection mismatch: ProviderFactory.get_provider selects the OAuthAccount with an ordered/filtered query (expires_at DESC, is_active==True) while GBPAuthManager._refresh_token selects with an unordered, unfiltered .first() — for any org with two or more OWNER/ADMIN OAuth accounts these can resolve to different rows, so the token gets refreshed on one row while the caller keeps using a stale token from another, causing repeated 401s / refresh churn. The async HTTP client does not retry 5xx errors and applies exponential backoff for 429 with no jitter and while ignoring the parsed Retry-After header, hurting resilience under Google's frequent transient 5xx/throttling. Module-level caches (_account_id_cache, _warned_metrics) are shared across the threads pool (concurrency=10) and mutated with non-atomic check-then-del patterns that can raise KeyError. The account-id cache is keyed only by google_location_id with no organization scoping. There is a large block of dead/duplicated legacy code in core/gbp_client.py (GBPClient class) that re-implements OAuth/token logic divergently from the live provider. Lower-severity issues include unchecked KeyErrors on token-exchange JSON, a docstring/method mismatch, and a reply path that returns success without inspecting the API response. No raw token logging was found (tokens travel in headers, not URLs; Google error bodies don't contain tokens).

areaSummaries.label: backend: models / DB / sessions / migrations
areaSummaries.summary: The models/DB/migrations area is generally well-structured: org_id is consistently FK-cascaded, billing/credit read-modify-writes correctly use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, the alembic DAG resolves to a single clean head, and the new location_media/invoice_url migrations are coherent with their models (enum values_callable matches the PG enum, server_defaults present). The most significant gap is in the new location_media feature: there is no unique constraint on (location_id, media_key), and the reconcile task (sync_location_media_task) upserts by media_key in Python with no advisory lock, so concurrent syncs / a sync racing the publish confirm-by-list can insert duplicate gallery rows. Secondary issues are several missing indexes on frequently-filtered FK columns (users.organization_id, sync_logs.organization_id/location_id, oauth_accounts.user_id, invites.organization_id), a non-reversible/data-unsafe ADD COLUMN NOT NULL without server_default in the post_media upgrade migration, a missing uniqueness guard on oauth_accounts that the auth upsert assumes, and minor redundancy (duplicate index over a composite PK).

areaSummaries.label: backend: LLM (ai reply, sentiment)
areaSummaries.summary: The LLM area is reasonably defensive in places (credit is deducted only after a successful generation, review comments are XML-escaped in the AI-reply path, output labels are validated against an allow-list before persistence, and the AI-reply endpoint surfaces LLM failures as a clean 502). However there are several real issues concentrated in the sentiment path: review text is NOT escaped before being interpolated into the batch sentiment prompt (the variable is misleadingly named "safe_comment"), allowing prompt/structure injection that can spoof review IDs and corrupt sentiment labels within a location's batch; sentiment tagging has no cost controls and a self-amplifying retry topology (per-chunk re-enqueue of the whole-location task plus an hourly beat sweep) that can fan out unbounded paid Groq calls when the LLM is unhealthy or output is unparseable; max_tokens=300 for batches of 15 reviews makes JSON truncation likely, which silently drops the whole batch and feeds the infinite-retry loop; and an empty GROQ_API_KEY is masked with a dummy key so misconfiguration manifests as runtime 401 loops instead of failing fast. The async sentiment function also blocks with time.sleep, batch-size docstrings contradict the code, and process_review_sentiment_task is dead code that hides failures behind a "completed" status.

areaSummaries.label: backend: sync & domain services
areaSummaries.summary: The sync & domain services are generally well-structured (org-scoped queries, idempotent upserts, optimistic-concurrency + row locks on the listing-edit state machine, atomic commits in review sync). However I found several real correctness and robustness defects: a Celery task is dispatched before the surrounding transaction commits in review sync (ordering/visibility bug), the media validator has no decompression-bomb / pixel guard (DoS on the threaded worker), the public invite-verification GET mutates and commits state on every call, the URL validator is far too permissive and accepts scheme-less/invalid URLs that GBP will later reject, the JSON/structured-object validators accept arbitrary shapes for critical fields (address) with no schema check, and the business-hours validator never validates closeDay or that close > open. None are cross-tenant leaks — multi-tenant isolation and RBAC field-permission checks hold up. Findings are ordered by impact.

areaSummaries.label: backend: config / app wiring / security headers / CORS / docker
areaSummaries.summary: The config/wiring/security/docker area has one dominant, critical flaw: APP_ENV is never set anywhere (not in docker-compose.yml, not in .env.example), and config.py defaults it to "development". Every security control in the app is gated on `APP_ENV != "development"`, so a deployment built from these artifacts silently runs in dev mode — CSRF is disabled, the production secret-validation guards are skipped, HSTS is dropped, and localhost CORS origins are injected. Compounding this, the single docker-compose.yml is dev-shaped (uvicorn --reload, source-mounted volume) yet marked restart: always as if it were the production deployment. Security headers and the non-root Dockerfile user are solid positives, but several API handlers leak raw exception text to clients, there is no rate limiting anywhere, dependencies are unpinned (>=), and a weak placeholder JWT_SECRET/ENCRYPTION_KEY ships in .env.example. Findings are ordered by exploitability.

areaSummaries.label: frontend: auth / API client / session / CSRF
areaSummaries.summary: The frontend auth design is mostly sound: tokens live in httpOnly cookies (no localStorage/XSS exposure), the API client consistently uses `credentials: 'include'`, CSRF uses a double-submit cookie validated server-side, and a single-flight `refreshPromise` prevents refresh stampedes. The most serious problem is a cookie-attribute mismatch: after a token refresh the client rewrites the `gmb_csrf_token` cookie with `SameSite=Lax` and no `Secure` flag, which contradicts the backend's `SameSite=None; Secure` and breaks cross-site delivery in the production (Vercel-frontend + separate-API) topology — leading to CSRF 403s on every mutating request that follows a refresh. Secondary issues: protected routes are guarded only client-side (no Next.js middleware), error details from the backend are echoed into the login URL, two export calls bypass the central client (no 401 refresh), CSRF is fully disabled in development alongside a mock-auth bypass, and the API base URL silently falls back to a localhost default. Findings ordered by impact.

areaSummaries.label: frontend: data fetching / React Query / state
areaSummaries.summary: Data-fetching bugs. Also (low): FE-DATA-7 UpgradeModal:42 useQuote fires per +/- click no debounce; FE-DATA-8 useLocationWorkspace:126 optimistic reject sets 'Failed' (==publish fail); FE-DATA-9 ProfileTab:20 ['field-configs'] unscoped global key; FE-DATA-10 UpgradeModal/TopUpModal/RemandateBanner Razorpay handlers swallow confirmPayment errors via empty catch and close modal optimistically.

areaSummaries.label: frontend: dashboard pages & components correctness
areaSummaries.summary: The dashboard frontend is generally well-built (good empty states, loading skeletons, abort-safe polling with interval cleanup, RBAC-gated actions, ErrorBoundary present). However there are several real correctness bugs: an off-by-range date computation on the org Insights page that under/over-shoots the query window across month boundaries; a stale-closure dependency gap in the Posts campaign-polling effect that can leave terminal campaigns polling forever; timezone-naive date parsing in relative-time helpers that can render "in the future"/negative durations; and a list-key correctness issue where keyword/leaderboard rows are keyed by array index across sort/pagination. None are cross-tenant/security holes (org scoping is enforced server-side; the audited pages only render server-filtered data). No dangerouslySetInnerHTML/XSS sinks were found. Findings below are ordered by impact.

areaSummaries.label: frontend: billing / payment UI (Razorpay)
areaSummaries.summary: The Razorpay billing UI is reasonably structured: prices/credits/amounts are all computed server-side (the client-passed `credits` in TopUpModal and `locationCount` in UpgradeModal are display-only; the backend derives the charge from `pack_key`/`location_count`), and final activation is gated on a backend signature-verified `/billing/confirm` call plus a webhook backstop. So there is no client-trusted-amount or "success without backend verification" hole. However there is a systemic double-submit / double-order weakness: every "pay" button is disabled only by the create-order mutation's `isPending`, which resets to false the instant the order/subscription is created and before the Razorpay modal actually opens, and `openRazorpay` is never awaited — so a second click creates a second Razorpay subscription/order (and `create_subscription_checkout` overwrites `org.razorpay_subscription_id` with no idempotency). Compounding this, all four confirm handlers swallow confirm() errors (including a genuine 400 "Invalid payment signature") behind an optimistic "Payment received!" toast, and the Razorpay script-load failure path throws into an unawaited promise so the user sees nothing. These are high/medium UX-and-money-adjacent bugs rather than direct exploits.

confirmed.title: Cross-tenant IDOR: location health-score endpoint has no organization_id filter
confirmed.description: GET /locations/{location_id}/health-score uses require_location_access, which for org-wide roles (Owner/Admin, and org-scoped Viewer) returns the path location_id WITHOUT any org-boundary check (deps.py get_user_location_ids returns None for ADMIN_ROLES, so the `location_id not in allowed_location_ids` guard is skipped). The handler then queries LocationHealthScore directly by raw location_id with no organization_id scoping, and on a miss calls HealthScoreService.recalculate_health_score(db, location_id) which itself does `db.query(Location).filter(Location.id == location_id)` with no org filter. An Admin/Owner of Org A can pass a location_id belonging to Org B and read its health score/label AND trigger a recalculation write against Org B's row. LocationHealthScore has no organization_id column, so the only correct scoping is a join to an org-filtered Location, which this endpoint omits — unlike every sibling endpoint (get_location, get_location_sla, get_location_sync_status) which all filter `Location.organization_id == current_user.organization_id`.
confirmed.evidence:
score = db.query(LocationHealthScore).filter(LocationHealthScore.location_id == location_id).first()
    if not score:
        score = HealthScoreService.recalculate_health_score(db, location_id, "manual")  # no org filter anywhere
# require_location_access docstring: "This intentionally enforces ONLY location scope, not org existence — handlers keep their own org-filtered query for the 404" — but this handler has NO org-filtered query.
confirmed.recommendation: Add an org-boundary check before reading/recalculating: first `location = db.query(Location).filter(Location.id == location_id, Location.organization_id == current_user.organization_id).first()` and 404 if missing; pass that org-validated location_id onward. Alternatively scope the LocationHealthScore query via a join to Location filtered by current_user.organization_id, and have recalculate_health_score accept/enforce an organization_id.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified by reading all cited code paths. (1) backend/app/api/locations.py:363-380 (get_location_health_score) queries db.query(LocationHealthScore).filter(LocationHealthScore.location_id == location_id) with NO organization_id filter, and on miss calls HealthScoreService.recalculate_health_score(db, location_id, "manual"). (2) require_location_access (deps.py:119-141) calls get_user_location_ids, which returns None for ADMIN_ROLES (lines 82-83) and org-scoped Viewers (lines 84-85); when None, the guard `if allowed_location_ids is not None and location_id not in allowed_location_ids` is skipped, so an arbitrary path location_id passes through for Owner/Admin and org-Viewer with zero org-boundary check. The dependency's own docstring states it enforces ONLY location scope and relies on the handler keeping an org-filtered query for the 404 — but this handler has none. (3) HealthScoreService.recalculate_health_score (health_score_service.py:16) does db.query(Location).filter(Location.id == location_id).first() with no organization_id filter, then writes/updates the LocationHealthScore row (lines 182-198 via db.flush, committed by the endpoint at locations.py:378) — so this is both a cross-tenant READ and a WRITE against another org's row. (4) The LocationHealthScore model (location_health_score.py) has location_id but no organization_id column, confirming the only correct scoping is a join to an org-filtered Location, which the endpoint omits. (5) Every sibling endpoint — get_location (204-207), get_location_sla (106-109), enable_location_sla (123-126), get_location_sync_status (325-328) — adds Location.organization_id == current_user.organization_id; the health-score endpoint is the lone exception. Reproducible: an Owner/Admin (or org-scoped Viewer for read-only) of Org A can pass Org B's location_id to read its health score/label/recommendations and trigger a recalculation write to Org B's data. This is a genuine cross-tenant IDOR. Severity confirmed high per the project's stated multi-tenant isolation invariant (missing organization_id filter => IDOR / cross-tenant leak = high-severity); it requires an authenticated org-admin and the leaked data is business-profile health metrics rather than credentials/PII, but the cross-tenant write capability and clear isolation break justify high.

confirmed.title: Subscription and location-addon refunds never reclaim quota or per-location credits (money-loss / abuse path)
confirmed.description: On refund.created/refund.processed, only `topup_charge` refunds are reversed. For `subscription_charge` and `location_addon` the handler merely logs 'need MANUAL reconciliation' and leaves org.location_quota, org.monthly_ai_credits_balance and the unlocked locations' billing_status='active' fully intact. A user can pay for a subscription or add-on locations, consume the granted AI credits and run paid syncs/posts, then obtain a refund through Razorpay/their bank and keep all entitlements indefinitely until a human notices. Because the handler returns success, the org continues billing/serving as if paid.
confirmed.evidence: `if txn.transaction_type == "topup_charge" and txn.credits: org.topup_ai_credits_balance = max(0, ...)` ... `else: logger.warning("Refund of %s payment %s for org %s grants quota/credits that need MANUAL reconciliation ...")` — no quota decrement, no re-lock, no credit clawback.
confirmed.recommendation: For location_addon refunds, decrement location_quota by notes['added'], re-lock the specific location_ids to pending_payment, and reduce monthly credits accordingly. For subscription refunds, move the org to past_due/locked or set subscription_ends_at. At minimum, raise an alert/flag the org as disputed so it stops serving paid features automatically.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified against backend/app/services/billing/webhook_service.py and the lifecycle sweeps. In _handle_refund (lines 297-327), only txn.transaction_type == "topup_charge" is reversed (decrements topup_ai_credits_balance, lines 318-321). For every other type (subscription_charge, location_addon) the else branch (lines 322-327) ONLY logs a warning ("...need MANUAL reconciliation...") and returns; it never touches org.subscription_status, plan, location_quota, monthly_ai_credits_balance, paid_location_quota, grace_period_ends_at, subscription_ends_at, nor re-locks any Location. So the entitlements granted earlier remain: apply_subscription_charged sets plan="active"/subscription_status="active" and monthly_ai_credits_balance (lines 171-212); _handle_location_addon_captured flips locations to billing_status="active", bumps location_quota and adds granted*CREDITS_PER_LOCATION credits (lines 429-445). I confirmed no other mitigation exists: (a) EntitlementService.is_org_locked (entitlement_service.py 13-42) returns False for an active org with no subscription_ends_at in the past — a refund sets none of those fields, so the org stays unlocked; (b) EntitlementService.transition_expired_subscriptions (45-91) only locks on trial_ends_at / grace_period_ends_at / subscription_ends_at, none of which a refund populates; (c) enforce_upi_remandate_grace_task (tasks.py 556-626) only re-locks when subscription_needs_remandate is True, which a refund never sets. A grep for refund|dispute|chargeback across backend confirms _handle_refund is the ONLY refund path and there is no dispute/chargeback webhook handler at all. Net: after a subscription or add-on refund the org keeps quota, credits, and active locations and continues serving paid features (sync/posts/AI) indefinitely until a human reads the warning log. The exploit is real and reproducible. Severity held at high: it directly violates the stated billing-integrity invariant (paid ops gated on billing_status/credits) and creates an automated money-loss/free-service path. It is not bumped beyond high because triggering it requires the attacker to actually obtain a refund/chargeback (a manual, traceable, friction-heavy action) and the event is at least logged for manual reconciliation rather than being a fully silent leak.

confirmed.title: publish_job lock TTL (120s) shorter than the work allows lock expiry and a duplicate Google post
confirmed.description: process_publish_job_task takes r.lock(timeout=120) then runs provider.create_post (OAuth refresh + GBP create), which under slowness exceeds 120s; the lease expires, the lock auto-releases, and a Celery retry re-acquires it and calls create_post AGAIN, double-publishing to Google. The campaign-shard path (1299-1349) has NO per-job lock at all. All releases swallow LockNotOwnedError via try/except pass.
confirmed.evidence: lock = r.lock(lock_key, timeout=120); res = run_async(provider.create_post(...)); finally: try: lock.release() except Exception: pass
confirmed.recommendation: Size the TTL above worst-case or extend the lease during the call. Add an idempotency guard against Google (skip if job.google_post_id set). Add a per-job lock or atomic UPDATE in the shard path. Log LockNotOwnedError.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified against the actual code. tasks.py:739 acquires lock = r.lock(lock_key, timeout=120) using core/redis_client.py get_redis() (a plain redis.Redis with no watchdog). There is NO lock.extend()/reacquire() anywhere in the publish path (grep confirmed), so the 120s lease is fixed wall-clock and auto-expires while work proceeds. The work under the lock (tasks.py:776 run_async(provider.create_post(...))) can realistically exceed 120s: providers/gbp/client.py request() retries up to max_retries=5 with httpx timeout=30.0 per attempt plus backoff sleeps 1+2+4+8s, so a single GBP call can take ~165s; create_post (provider.py:402) additionally does get_valid_token (OAuth refresh: auth.py lock blocking_timeout=10 + 10s POST) and _resolve_account_id (provider.py:93, which itself issues paginated GBP GETs through the same retrying client) before the POST localPosts. So TTL < worst-case work is real. Idempotency claim confirmed: job.google_post_id is only ever WRITTEN (lines 780, 827, 843, 853, 1327, 1339) and never read as a skip guard; the only re-entry guard (line 748) checks status in [PENDING, RETRYING], so a job that already succeeded on Google but lost its DB commit / lost its lock will be re-published. Concurrent re-dispatch is realistic: the scheduled sweeper (line 1885-1893) re-dispatches process_publish_job_task for pending posts, and self.retry(max_retries=3) re-enqueues the same job_id; once the lease expires the blocking=False acquire (line 741) will succeed for the racing instance, calling create_post AGAIN -> duplicate Google post. Shard path confirmed to have NO per-job lock at all (lines 1265-1427): it only does a non-atomic status read + UPDATE to RUNNING (line 1306), no Redis lock and no SELECT FOR UPDATE, so two shard tasks for the same job_id (e.g. the retry re-enqueue at 1395 plus the sweeper) can both publish. Release swallowing confirmed (lines 956-959: try: lock.release() except Exception: pass), which also hides LockNotOwnedError. All four sub-claims hold. Kept severity high: the outcome is a real, externally-visible duplicate post to a customer's Google Business Profile with no idempotency backstop, and the shard path's complete absence of locking makes it worse than the single-job path alone; not raised to critical because it is a reliability/correctness defect, not data corruption or a tenant-isolation/security breach.

confirmed.title: max_tokens=300 too small for 15-review batches → JSON truncation silently drops the whole batch
confirmed.description: Batches are built from chunks of 15 reviews, but the LLM call caps completion at max_tokens=300. A single JSON object like {"id": 1234567, "sentiment": "Negative", "issue_category": "Product Quality"} is ~25-35 tokens; 15 of them plus array punctuation easily exceeds 300 tokens. When the array is truncated mid-output, json.loads(cleaned) raises JSONDecodeError, the handler logs and `return`s, and NONE of the 15 reviews get sentiment_tagged_at set. Those reviews stay NULL forever, so the hourly beat re-enqueues them again, hits the same truncation, and burns Groq quota indefinitely without ever making progress.
confirmed.evidence:
chunks: list[list[Review]] = [untagged[i:i + 15] for i in range(0, len(untagged), 15)]
...
raw = await llm.complete(SYSTEM_PROMPT, user_message, max_tokens=300, temperature=0.1)
...
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    logger.error("Failed to parse LLM JSON response for sentiment batch: %s", str(e))
    return
confirmed.recommendation: Size max_tokens to the batch (e.g. ~40 tokens/review → batch_size*40 with a floor), or reduce the chunk size to match the budget, or both. Also add salvage on truncation (e.g. parse the longest valid JSON prefix / use a streaming-tolerant extractor) so a partial batch still tags the reviews it can, instead of dropping all 15 and looping.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified against the actual code. backend/app/services/sentiment_service.py:61 builds chunks of 15 reviews (untagged[i:i+15]) and line 107 calls llm.complete(..., max_tokens=300). In backend/app/llm/groq.py:13-24, max_tokens is passed straight to Groq's chat.completions.create as the hard completion-token cap. Each output object {"id": <int>, "sentiment": "...", "issue_category": "..."} is ~25-40 tokens with the OpenAI/Groq tokenizer; 15 of them plus array punctuation runs ~350-600 tokens, comfortably over 300. So a full 15-item chunk truncates mid-array. Lines 121-125 then hit json.loads -> JSONDecodeError, log, and return with NO salvage (no longest-valid-prefix parse, no per-item fallback), so none of the 15 reviews get sentiment_tagged_at set. The loop is also confirmed: tag_reviews_sentiment_task (tasks.py:665-668) re-queries sentiment_tagged_at IS NULL, and retry_failed_sentiment_beat_task runs hourly (worker.py:67-70, schedule 3600.0) re-enqueuing every location that still has untagged reviews, so the same truncation repeats forever, burning Groq quota with zero progress. The claim is accurate and the cited evidence matches. Kept at high (not critical): the catastrophic full-truncation only triggers when a chunk is near-full (15). The normal event-driven path process_review_sentiment_task (tasks.py:705) tags single reviews (batch of 1, well under 300 tokens) and succeeds, so steady-state ingestion mostly avoids it; the failure bites on backfill/catch-up backlogs (initial large sync, or accumulated untagged reviews after a worker/LLM outage). Impact is lost enrichment plus an indefinite quota-burning loop, but no data corruption, tenant-isolation breach, or user-facing crash — so high, not critical, is correct.

confirmed.title: APP_ENV is never set, so every deployment defaults to development mode and disables CSRF, secret validation, and HSTS
confirmed.description: config.py declares `APP_ENV: str = "development"`. The string `APP_ENV` does not appear anywhere in docker-compose.yml (the only compose file) and is not present in .env.example. Because settings are loaded from env/.env, every container built from these artifacts boots with APP_ENV="development". Critically, the entire security posture is gated on this single value: check_csrf returns early when APP_ENV=='development' (deps.py:154), the JWT_SECRET/ENCRYPTION_KEY/Razorpay fatal validators only fire when APP_ENV != 'development' (config.py:53,111), HSTS is only emitted when not development (main.py:62), and dev localhost CORS origins are injected (main.py:27). So a 'production' deploy from this repo silently runs with CSRF fully disabled for all mutating requests, no enforcement that JWT/ENCRYPTION/Razorpay secrets are set, no HSTS, and http://localhost:3000 + 127.0.0.1:3000 added as allowed credentialed CORS origins.
confirmed.evidence: config.py:15  `APP_ENV: str = "development"`  — and a repo-wide grep for APP_ENV in docker-compose.yml returns 'No matches found', and .env.example has no APP_ENV line. deps.py:153-155  `from app.core.config import settings\n    if settings.APP_ENV == "development":\n        return`
confirmed.recommendation: Make production the safe default: change the default to `APP_ENV: str = "production"` and/or fail closed by requiring APP_ENV to be explicitly one of {development,staging,production}. Add `APP_ENV=production` to docker-compose env blocks for backend/worker/beat and document it in .env.example. Better: gate security controls on an explicit `APP_ENV == 'production'` opt-OUT rather than an opt-IN, so a missing/typo'd value never disables CSRF/HSTS.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified every cited line against the actual code. config.py:15 declares `APP_ENV: str = "development"` (unsafe default). confirmed.title: Client rewrites CSRF cookie with SameSite=Lax / no Secure after refresh, breaking cross-site requests
confirmed.description: After a successful /auth/refresh, the client overwrites the gmb_csrf_token cookie from JavaScript using `samesite=lax` and omitting the `Secure` attribute. In production the SPA (Vercel) and API are on different registrable domains, so the backend deliberately issues this cookie as `SameSite=None; Secure` (see backend/app/api/auth.py:394-402). A `SameSite=Lax` cookie is NOT sent on cross-site fetch() requests, so the very next mutating request reads no/stale CSRF cookie and the backend double-submit check (backend/app/api/deps.py:170-184) fails with 403. This JS write is also redundant because /auth/refresh already returns the new token via a proper Set-Cookie header; the client write only downgrades it. Net effect: silent CSRF failures / broken mutations for any user whose 15-minute access token expired and was refreshed mid-session.
confirmed.recommendation: Delete the manual document.cookie write entirely and rely on the Set-Cookie returned by /auth/refresh (it already sets the correct attributes). If a JS-side write must be kept for symmetry, mirror the backend exactly: detect HTTPS and emit `; SameSite=None; Secure` in production so the cookie is delivered on cross-site requests.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified all three cited locations against actual code.

1) frontend/lib/api.ts:32-37 — After a successful /auth/refresh, the client does `document.cookie = \`gmb_csrf_token=${data.csrf_token}; path=/; max-age=...; samesite=lax\``. This write omits the `Secure` attribute and uses `samesite=lax`, exactly as claimed.

2) backend/app/api/auth.py:446-467 (the /refresh handler) — Confirms the backend already sets gmb_csrf_token via a real Set-Cookie header with `secure=secure_cookie` and `samesite=samesite_val`, where `secure_cookie = settings.FRONTEND_URL.startswith("https://")` and `samesite_val = "none" if secure_cookie else "lax"`. So in production (HTTPS Vercel) the backend issues `SameSite=None; Secure`. It ALSO returns the same value in the JSON body (`"csrf_token": csrf_token`), so the JS write is purely redundant. Because both writes use the same value, only the cookie ATTRIBUTES differ, and the browser keeps attributes from the last document.cookie write — downgrading the cookie to `SameSite=Lax` and non-Secure.

3) backend/app/api/deps.py:170-184 — Confirms the double-submit CSRF check: it reads the `gmb_csrf_token` cookie and compares to the `X-CSRF-Token` header, raising 403 if the cookie is missing or mismatched. A `SameSite=Lax` cookie is not transmitted on cross-site (different registrable domain) fetch() requests, so the next mutating request would carry no cookie → 403. request() in api.ts injects the header from getCookie() on POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE (lines 70-79), and getCookie reads document.cookie, so the SPA depends on this cookie being readable AND cross-site-deliverable.

Caveats checked: (a) deps.py:154 skips CSRF entirely when APP_ENV=="development", and (b) deps.py:161 lists /api/v1/auth/refresh in _CSRF_EXCLUDED_PATHS — so the downgraded cookie does not break refresh itself, only the subsequent mutating requests, and only in production cross-site HTTPS. This matches the finding's stated conditions precisely. The JS write can only ever downgrade SameSite from None→Lax and drop Secure; it can never improve cross-site delivery, so it is a genuine regression with no upside.

Impact: every user whose 15-minute access token expires and gets refreshed mid-session will have their CSRF cookie silently downgraded, breaking all subsequent mutations (403) in production cross-site deployments. The recommendation (delete the JS write; rely on Set-Cookie) is correct. Severity high is appropriate: it silently breaks core write functionality and undermines the CSRF control's correct operation post-refresh, though it is not itself a data-exposure/privilege-escalation vuln and the fix is trivial.

confirmed.title: attach_media trusts client-supplied storage_key/cdn_url enabling cross-tenant storage reference
confirmed.description: POST /posts/{id}/media (attach_media) creates a PostMedia row entirely from client-controlled PostMediaCreateRequest fields (storage_provider, storage_key, cdn_url, sha256_hash, width/height) with no validation that the referenced asset belongs to the caller's organization. While organization_id is forced to the caller's org, a tenant can supply `storage_key=uploads/org_<OTHER>/media/...` and the corresponding `cdn_url` of another tenant's stored object, attach it to their own post, and then publish it to Google — referencing/exfiltrating another org's private uploaded asset. There is no server-side ownership check tying cdn_url/storage_key back to a PostMedia the caller actually uploaded.

    organization_id=organization_id,
    storage_key=storage_key,            # client-supplied, e.g. uploads/org_OTHER/...
    cdn_url=str(media_data.cdn_url),     # client-supplied URL, never validated to caller's org
    sha256_hash=media_data.sha256_hash,
    ...)
db.add(media)
confirmed.recommendation: Require attach_media to reference an existing PostMedia id owned by the caller's organization (like location_media does with source_media_id + org filter), or validate that storage_key starts with `uploads/org_{organization_id}/` and that cdn_url maps to an asset row owned by this org. Reject any externally-controlled storage path that doesn't belong to the tenant.

VERIFIED the root defect is real. attach_media (backend/app/services/post_service.py:151-194) builds a PostMedia row entirely from client-supplied PostMediaCreateRequest fields. organization_id is forced to the caller's org (line 175), but storage_key (line 178) and cdn_url (line 186) are taken verbatim from the request with NO check that the referenced asset belongs to the caller's org. PostMediaCreateRequest (schemas/posts.py:202-213) accepts arbitrary storage_key and cdn_url. So a tenant CAN register a row whose organization_id=their own but whose storage_key=uploads/org_<OTHER>/media/<hash>.jpg and cdn_url=<victim public URL>. The legitimate upload path (api/media.py:80) derives storage_key server-side from the caller's org, confirming the safe contract attach_media violates.

However, the prior auditor's PRIMARY claimed impact (attach foreign asset, publish to Google, exfiltrate) is largely MITIGATED and overstated. confirmed.title: Credit/charge idempotency has no DB-level unique constraint on razorpay_payment_id; relies solely on app-level read-then-insert under an org lock
confirmed.description: Every money-bearing grant path (subscription charge, top-up, location add-on) enforces 'apply exactly once' with a read-then-write: `already = db.query(BillingTransaction).filter(BillingTransaction.razorpay_payment_id == payment_id).first(); if already: return` followed by `db.add(BillingTransaction(...))`. The only reason this is safe today is that every grant path first locks the org row with `select(Organization)...with_for_update()`, which serializes same-org webhook + reconcile + periodic-task deliveries. That invariant is undocumented and unenforced: any new grant path (or a refactor that drops the lock) silently re-enables double-credit/double-charge on webhook redelivery or a webhook+/confirm race. The webhook-event table's unique key protects the webhook path but the /confirm reconcile path writes NO event marker, so the payment_id check is the sole guard there.

This makes idempotency a DB guarantee independent of the org row lock.

confirmed.title: Proration uses integer .days truncation, systematically undercharging add-ons and zeroing out near cycle end
confirmed.description: _cycle_days_remaining computes `days_left = (reset - now).days`, which truncates toward zero. A location unlocked with 29 days, 23 hours remaining is billed for 29 days (loses ~1 day every time), and one unlocked with <24h remaining yields days_left=0 → prorated_addon_paise returns 0, so the user pays only the _MIN_ORDER_PAISE floor (₹1) to unlock a location that will be active for the entire next full cycle until the renewal plan-change takes effect. Combined across all add-ons this is a consistent revenue leak, and the last-day case is an exploitable cheap-unlock window.
confirmed.evidence: Line 277: `days_left = (reset - now).days` then `return max(0, min(days_left, days_in_cycle)), days_in_cycle`. Verified: for reset 23h away `.days` == 0; for 30d away `.days` == 29.
confirmed.recommendation: Use ceiling of the remaining fraction: `secs = (reset - now).total_seconds(); days_left = max(0, math.ceil(secs / 86400))`, or compute the prorated amount directly from total_seconds to avoid day truncation. Also ensure a brand-new add-on still bills at least the next renewal delta when days_left is ~0.

Verified in backend/app/services/billing/subscription_service.py line 277: `days_left = (reset - now).days`. Python's timedelta.days truncates the sub-day fraction toward zero for positive deltas — I confirmed by execution: 29d23h -> 29, 30d exact -> 30, 23h -> 0, 1d1h -> 1. So a location with 29d23h remaining is billed for 29 days (loses ~1 day), exactly as claimed.

Traced the consumer chain. quote_location_unlock (lines 297-301) calls PricingService.prorated_addon_paise(current_quota, added, interval, days_left, days_in_cycle) which (pricing_service.py lines 61-77) computes round(marginal * days_left / days_in_cycle). With days_left=0 the prorated amount is 0, then quote_location_unlock floors it to _MIN_ORDER_PAISE (100 paise = Rs 1) via max(amount, _MIN_ORDER_PAISE) on line 301. So the last-day case is a genuine Rs 1 unlock.

Confirmed the unlock really grants a full cycle: webhook_service.py _handle_location_addon_captured (lines 394-463) flips billing_status to 'active' immediately on payment.captured, grants the FULL per-location credits (not prorated, lines 444-445), bumps location_quota, and only schedules the recurring amount increase at cycle_end via update_subscription_plan_for_quota (subscription_service.py lines 376-379, schedule_change_at='cycle_end'). So paying Rs 1 in the final <24h of a cycle yields an active location plus full credits immediately and through the entire next full cycle before the higher renewal applies. Both the systematic-undercharge claim and the exploitable cheap-unlock claim are accurate.

This is a real revenue/abuse leak but not an isolation/security defect, so claimed 'medium' is correct. The recommended fix (math.ceil of remaining fraction, or compute from total_seconds, plus a sane minimum when days_left ~0) is appropriate.

confirmed.title: process_webhook returns HTTP 200 for unhandled/ignored events but raises 500 on business errors, and a fetch failure inside payment.captured silently no-ops the grant

Razorpay therefore considers the event delivered and will NOT retry, so a transient order-fetch failure permanently drops a paid top-up/add-on grant (only the eventually-run reconcile sweep can recover it). The idempotency marker is committed even though the business effect was skipped.

confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against backend/app/services/billing/webhook_service.py (_handle_payment_captured, lines 330-356) and process_webhook (lines 40-98), plus the caller billing.py:428-430 and the reconcile paths.

Back in process_webhook, since no exception propagates, db.commit() (line 88) persists the BillingWebhookEvent idempotency marker (added line 57), and the endpoint returns {"status":"ok"} = HTTP 200 (billing.py:430). Razorpay treats 200 as delivered and will not retry; the committed marker means even a redelivery is skipped as already-processed (lines 49-54). So a transient order-fetch failure permanently drops a paid top-up/add-on grant. The "200 for unhandled, 500 for business errors" half is also accurate (else branch at 85-86 logs and commits; raised exceptions roll back and re-raise at 93-98 -> 500).

One correction, in the WORSE direction: the finding says the reconcile sweep can recover it. The only scheduled reconcile (worker.py:72 reconcile_pending_subscriptions_task, tasks.py:513) reconciles SUBSCRIPTIONS only (reconcile_subscription). It never calls reconcile_topup_payment or reconcile_location_addon_payment; those run ONLY synchronously from the /billing/confirm endpoint (billing.py:153-159), driven by the frontend after checkout. So if the order-fetch fails AND the frontend confirm is missed/fails, the grant is permanently lost with no background safety net for these payment types.

Severity: raised from low/tech-debt to medium. Likelihood is low (needs a transient Razorpay order.fetch failure coinciding with a missed/failed frontend confirm), but the outcome is a direct financial-correctness defect — money captured, no credits/quota granted, no automatic recovery — which is customer-impacting rather than mere tech-debt. Recommendation (re-raise on order-fetch failure for empty-notes payment.captured so the marker rolls back and Razorpay retries) is sound.

confirmed.title: No task time limits + 1h visibility_timeout → long tasks get redelivered and run concurrently with themselves
confirmed.description: worker.py sets broker_transport_options['visibility_timeout']=3600 but configures NO task_time_limit / task_soft_time_limit and NO acks_late. With Celery's Redis broker, if a task is in-flight longer than the visibility timeout (1h) the broker re-delivers the same message to another of the 10 worker threads, which then executes the task a SECOND time concurrently. Tasks that can genuinely exceed an hour exist here: reconcile_pending_subscriptions_task loops a synchronous Razorpay API call over every pending org, sync_all_active_categories_metadata_task / sync_all_insights_beat_task fan out over all orgs, and backfill tasks loop one GBP get_location call per location. The only thing preventing double-processing is per-org/per-resource app locks whose own TTLs (e.g. publish locks=120s, sync_insights=300s) are SHORTER than 3600s, so the lock expires before the duplicate arrives.
confirmed.evidence: broker_transport_options={ 'visibility_timeout': 3600, ... } and the entire celery.conf.update(...) has no task_time_limit/task_soft_time_limit/acks_late. e.g. reconcile_pending_subscriptions_task comment itself admits: '30-min lease: this loops over all pending orgs making a synchronous Razorpay call each, which can exceed a 5-min TTL'.
confirmed.recommendation: Set explicit guards in worker.py: task_time_limit (hard kill, e.g. 1800s) and task_soft_time_limit (e.g. 1500s) so no task can outlive the 3600s visibility window, and consider raising visibility_timeout above the longest expected task. For the long fan-out/reconcile tasks specifically, make their Redis lock TTL >= the worst-case runtime (or refresh it periodically) so a redelivered duplicate is reliably skipped.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
VERIFIED the core config claim in backend/app/worker.py: broker_transport_options sets visibility_timeout=3600 (line 27); a grep over backend/ confirms there is NO task_time_limit, task_soft_time_limit, or acks_late anywhere. The Celery Redis-transport redelivery mechanic is described correctly: a message not acked within visibility_timeout becomes visible and is redelivered, and since worker.py runs --pool=threads --concurrency=10 the duplicate runs concurrently with the still-in-flight original in the same process. So the underlying risk is genuine and not mitigated by any time limit.

However the finding's specifics are partly inaccurate, which lowers severity from high to medium:

1) reconcile_pending_subscriptions_task (tasks.py:513-553): CONFIRMED it loops a synchronous SubscriptionService.reconcile_subscription (Razorpay call) per pending org; its own inline comment (lines 525-526) admits the concurrency risk. Lock TTL=1800s (line 527), which is HALF the 3600 window, so an actual 3600s+ run requires the pending set (orgs with a razorpay_subscription_id but not active/locked) to be very large — an unusual, large-scale condition.

2) sync_all_insights_beat_task (2502) and sync_all_active_categories_metadata_task (2580): the finding MISCHARACTERIZES these. Both are pure enqueuers — a DB query plus .delay() in a loop with NO synchronous external API call in the body. They finish in seconds and effectively cannot approach 3600s. The per-org/per-category work happens in the fanned-out child tasks, not here.

3) backfill_google_category_resource_names_task (2725-2759): the finding is CORRECT — it loops provider.get_location() (a synchronous GBP API call) per location across ALL orgs with NO lock at all, so a redelivered duplicate would run the whole backfill again. This is the strongest concrete example, but it's an ad-hoc/one-off backfill, not a beat-scheduled task.

4) Per-org workers sync_locations_task (line 221) and sync_organization_insights_task (line 2400) use 3600s locks — EQUAL to the visibility window, not shorter as the finding implies ('locks whose TTLs are SHORTER than 3600s'). That equality is a real boundary bug (lock expires exactly when redelivery fires, so the duplicate can re-acquire), but it is a tight edge case rather than the general short-lock claim stated.

Net: the mechanism is real and the recommendation (add task_time_limit < visibility_timeout, and size long-task locks to worst-case runtime) is valid defense-in-depth. But triggering it requires large scale plus a slow external API, the two named beat fan-out tasks don't actually qualify, and the sync locks are 3600 (=window) not shorter. That makes real-world impact for this MVP medium rather than high.

confirmed.title: Insights org-sync marks itself complete and evaluates attention flags before per-location syncs have run

confirmed.title: campaign retry double-counts pending_shards if the worker dies between the NX guard and re-enqueue
confirmed.description: Campaign shard completion is tracked by an integer Redis counter campaign:{id}:pending_shards that is decremented per finished shard; when it hits 0 the terminal transition fires. On a retryable job failure the code does r.set(retry_key, nx=True) then r.incr(pending_shards) then process_campaign_shard_task.apply_async(...). The NX guard prevents the SAME retry from incrementing twice, but the incr and the apply_async are not atomic: if the worker crashes after r.incr(pending_shards) but before apply_async succeeds (or the broker rejects it), pending_shards is permanently > 0 and the campaign NEVER reaches the terminal transition (it hangs in 'Processing' forever with no timeout/sweeper). Conversely _decr_and_flush_terminal_state only acts on '== 0', so an over-decrement (e.g. duplicate shard execution from BE-CELERY-1) yields a negative value that also never equals 0.
confirmed.evidence: if r.set(retry_key, '1', ex=86400, nx=True):\n    r.incr(f"campaign:{campaign_id}:pending_shards")\n    process_campaign_shard_task.apply_async(args=([job_id], organization_id, campaign_id), countdown=countdown)  ... and terminal check 'if remaining_shards == 0:' only.
confirmed.recommendation: Enqueue the retry FIRST (apply_async) and only incr pending_shards after a confirmed enqueue, or use a Lua script to make incr+enqueue-intent atomic. Add a periodic reaper/beat that detects campaigns stuck in Processing past a deadline (pending_shards != 0 with no recent activity) and forces a terminal transition; treat remaining_shards <= 0 (not just == 0) as terminal.

Confirmed mechanics:
- Retry path (lines 1392-1398): retry_key = r.set(..., nx=True) guards duplicate retries, then INSIDE the if-block it does r.incr(campaign:{id}:pending_shards) (1394) followed by process_campaign_shard_task.apply_async(...) (1395-1398). These are two distinct, non-atomic operations: the counter is bumped first to account for the future retry shard, and the retry shard (which will later decrement it) is enqueued second.
- pending_shards is initialized to len(shards) at dispatch (line 1194) and the terminal transition fires only when r.decr() returns exactly 0 (line 1466: `if remaining_shards == 0:`). The original shard always decrements once in its outer finally via _decr_and_flush_terminal_state (line 1447).
- Failure window: if the worker dies, or the broker rejects/errors on apply_async at 1395, the incr at 1394 has already landed but no retry shard exists. The NX guard does NOT help recover — it only prevents a *second* incr for the same retry. The exception from apply_async is swallowed by the broad `except Exception as retry_err` at 1422 (just logs), so even a transient broker hiccup (no crash needed) permanently elevates the counter. On a true mid-task crash, default Celery acks_late=False (no override found anywhere in app — grep returned no matches) means the original shard task is NOT redelivered, so its own finally decrement at 1447 is also lost, compounding the stuck state.

Verified worker.py beat_schedule (lines 41-83) has NO campaign reaper/sweeper — there is no stuck-Processing recovery for campaigns (unlike listing_edits/location_media which DO have stale-recovery). So the claim that nothing rescues it is accurate.

The trigger requires a retryable job failure (already the degraded path) coinciding with a crash/broker error in a tiny window between incr and apply_async; underlying jobs are still recorded in Postgres, so the damage is to campaign terminal bookkeeping (campaign/primary_post stuck mid-state, requires manual Redis cleanup) rather than data loss or cross-tenant exposure. Not high (narrow coincident-failure window, no security/isolation impact), but genuinely real and unmitigated. Recommendation stands: enqueue before incr, or make incr+enqueue atomic (Lua), add a reaper beat, and treat remaining_shards <= 0 as terminal.

confirmed.title: Campaign progress counters have no TTL and can be resurrected after terminal flush, causing stuck campaigns
confirmed.description: Campaign counter keys use plain r.set with no expiry. Completion is detected only by r.decr hitting 0, which deletes all keys. If any shard task is lost (crash, broker redelivery dropped, eviction) the decr never happens, pending_shards never reaches 0, the campaign stays Processing forever and keys leak. incr on a deleted key recreates it from 0 to 1, so a late retry shard after the terminal flush resurrects pending_shards at 1 on a completed campaign, re-opening it permanently.
confirmed.evidence: r.set(campaign pending_shards, len(shards)); remaining_shards = r.decr(campaign pending_shards); if remaining_shards == 0: r.delete(campaign pending_shards)
confirmed.recommendation: Put a TTL on all campaign counter keys, refresh on each incr/decr, treat remaining_shards <= 0 as terminal, and set a done sentinel. Better: derive completion from the DB count of non-terminal PublishJobs.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
VERIFIED against backend/app/tasks.py, worker.py, and core/redis_client.py.

NO-TTL is confirmed: counter keys are set with plain r.set and no ex= at the two dispatch sites — orchestrate path (1194-1198: pending_shards/success/failed/total_locations/status) and scheduled-post path (1854-1855). redis_client.get_redis() sets no default expiry. The only TTL anywhere on a campaign key is the retry-dedup guard retry_key (1393, ex=86400), not the counters.

COMPLETION-VIA-DECR-ONLY is confirmed: _decr_and_flush_terminal_state (1464) does remaining_shards = r.decr(pending_shards) and only performs the terminal Postgres transition + key cleanup when remaining_shards == 0 (1466,1520-1524). There is no other completion path: I read worker.py beat_schedule (41-83) — there is NO reaper/watchdog/sweep task for stuck "Processing" campaigns, and grep for reap/watchdog/sweep/stuck/stale found none relevant. So if any shard never reaches its decr, pending_shards stays > 0 forever, the campaign is never transitioned out of Processing, and all 5 keys leak permanently.

LOST-SHARD is reachable: the decr lives in the task's finally block (1428-1447). Celery is configured with default acks_late=False (worker.py 13-35 sets no acks_late/task_reject_on_worker_lost), so on the Redis broker the message is acked at pickup; a hard worker death (SIGKILL/OOM — plausible with --pool=threads --concurrency=10 losing up to 10 in-flight shards) skips finally and is NOT redelivered (visibility_timeout only redelivers un-acked messages). This wedges the campaign in Processing permanently. CONFIRMED and reproducible.

RESURRECTION sub-claim is PARTLY OVERSTATED. The ordinary retry path is actually guarded: the retry's r.incr(pending_shards) (1394) executes synchronously inside the parent shard's per-job loop BEFORE the parent shard's own decr in finally (1447), and is further deduped by r.set(retry_key, nx=True). So a pending retry cannot let pending_shards hit 0 prematurely, and a normal retry does not resurrect a completed campaign. The factual claim that 'incr on a deleted key recreates it at 1' is true (Redis semantics), but it only matters as a downstream consequence of the lost-shard/stray-message edge, not the routine retry flow the finding emphasizes.

NET: the primary defect (no TTL + decr-gated completion + no reaper => one lost shard wedges the campaign forever and leaks keys) is genuine and not mitigated elsewhere. Severity adjusted high->medium: it is a degraded-mode-only failure triggered by worker hard-kill / broker anomaly (not a routine path), with no multi-tenant leak, data corruption, or billing impact; the recommendation (TTL + treat <=0 as terminal + DB-count-based completion / done sentinel) is appropriate.

confirmed.title: Un-pooled redis.from_url / aioredis.from_url clients leak a connection on every call
confirmed.description: Three paths build a Redis client via from_url with no shared pool, creating a fresh connection each call and never closing it: entitlement_service.get_redis_client, deps.get_redis_client (per HTTP request), and gbp/auth.py opening aioredis.from_url on every token refresh which never awaits aclose. Each leaks until GC, risking server-side exhaustion. decode_responses True here vs False in core means the same key returns str vs bytes by client.
confirmed.evidence: def get_redis_client(): return redis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL, decode_responses=True); gbp/auth.py: r = aioredis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL) -- never aclose'd
confirmed.recommendation: Consolidate on one shared pooled sync client and one aioredis pool; unify decode_responses; close aioredis via async with or aclose in finally; drop the duplicate pool in api/posts.py.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified all three cited paths plus the canonical pool in core/redis_client.py and the duplicate in api/posts.py.

PARTLY REAL, but the finding overstates impact and misreads two of the three paths:

1) gbp/auth.py:98 — GENUINE. `import redis.asyncio as aioredis` (line 60), `r = aioredis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL)` (line 98). The finally block (lines 247-251) only does `await lock.release()`; `r` is never `aclose()`'d on any code path (success, return-early, or except). An async redis client holds a connection pool + asyncio transport; relying on GC for async resources is unreliable and accumulates unclosed connections. This is a real resource-hygiene bug. It runs per OAuth token refresh (recurs as tokens near expiry, ~hourly per org), so it accumulates over time.

2) deps.py:186-187 — claim is WRONG. The finding says this leaks 'per HTTP request,' but get_redis_client here is used ONLY by check_location_quota (line 231), whose own docstring (lines 221-224) states it 'is currently unused,' and grep confirms check_location_quota is not wired into any route/Depends anywhere in app. So this per-request leak does not actually occur.

3) entitlement_service.py:7-8 — technically un-pooled, but only called from transition_expired_subscriptions (line 50), a low-frequency beat task. The sync redis-py Redis from from_url builds its own default ConnectionPool and is reclaimed on GC (sync redis-py closes the pool in __del__). Minor inefficiency, not exhaustion.

Technical correction to the premise: redis.from_url does NOT open a TCP connection per call — it constructs a client with a lazy pool; a connection opens on first command and returns to that instance's pool. So 'creating a fresh connection each call and never closing it' overstates the sync paths. The decode_responses=True (deps/entitlement) vs False (core/redis_client.py) inconsistency is real but is a separate correctness footnote, not part of the leak.

Net: the only reproducible leak is the never-closed aioredis client in gbp/auth.py; the deps path is dead code and the sync entitlement path is GC-reclaimed and low-frequency. The recommendation (consolidate on one pooled sync client + one aioredis pool, close async via aclose/async with, drop the duplicate posts.py pool) is sound. Given one bounded async leak with a GC backstop and the other two paths being non-issues, high is overstated; medium is appropriate.

confirmed.title: OAuth account selection differs between factory and refresh manager — token refresh can target the wrong row
confirmed.description: ProviderFactory.get_provider selects the org's OAuthAccount with `.order_by(OAuthAccount.expires_at.desc(), User.id.asc())` AND `User.is_active == True` (factory.py:46-50). GBPAuthManager._refresh_token selects the OAuthAccount for the SAME org with a bare `.first()` and NO ordering and NO is_active filter (auth.py:66-71, 117-121, 184-188). An organization can have multiple OWNER/ADMIN users each with an OAuthAccount (ADMIN_ROLES = {OWNER, ADMIN}; no uniqueness constraint exists on oauth_accounts per org). When >1 admin OAuth account exists, the factory hands the caller the token from row A (newest expiry, active) while the refresh path reads/writes row B (arbitrary DB order). The refresh then updates row B's tokens, the AuthContext is synced from row B, but the next ProviderFactory call still loads row A — so the access token effectively never refreshes for the caller, producing repeated 401s, redundant refreshes, and possible lockout.

At minimum add the identical `.order_by(OAuthAccount.expires_at.desc(), User.id.asc())` and `User.is_active == True` to all three queries in auth.py so the same row is consistently selected.

VERIFIED the query divergence is real. factory.py:39-50 (ProviderFactory.get_provider) selects the org's OAuthAccount with `.filter(User.organization_id==org, User.role.in_(ADMIN_ROLES), User.is_active==True, OAuthAccount.provider.in_([...])).order_by(OAuthAccount.expires_at.desc(), User.id.asc()).first()` — deterministic, newest-expiry, active-only. The three queries in auth.py `_refresh_token` (lines 67-71 quick-check, 117-121 post-lock check, 184-188 write phase) all use a bare `.join(User).filter(org, role.in(ADMIN_ROLES), provider.in([...])).first()` with NO order_by and NO `User.is_active` filter (the write query adds only `.with_for_update()`). So factory and refresh manager can resolve DIFFERENT rows.

PRECONDITION CONFIRMED: OAuthAccount (models/oauth_account.py) is keyed on user_id with no per-org/per-user uniqueness constraint; ADMIN_ROLES={Owner,Admin} (core/roles.py). Multiple owner/admin users per org each get an OAuthAccount (api/auth.py creates one per user; test tests/test_sync_rbac_regressions.py:160-188 explicitly builds owner+admin gbp OAuthAccounts in one org with different expiries). So >1 candidate row per org is realistic.

GENUINE HARMS that hold up: (1) the refresh path can pick an account belonging to an INACTIVE admin (factory filters is_active, refresh does not) — if that user's Google grant was revoked, the refresh raises PermanentAuthError and fails an operation that should have refreshed the active admin's still-valid grant. (2) The refresh reads/writes the wrong row (row B) relative to the row the factory selected (row A), causing redundant refreshes and oscillating selection across provider instances (after refreshing row B, row B becomes newest-expiry, so the next factory call flips to it), i.e. token churn.

BUT the finding OVERSTATES the impact. Its core claim — "the access token effectively never refreshes for the caller, producing repeated 401s and possible lockout" — does not hold. get_valid_token (auth.py:40-55) ALWAYS returns self.auth_context.access_token, and _refresh_token unconditionally syncs self.auth_context from whatever row it refreshed (lines 225-228) before returning. Within a provider instance (providers built fresh per operation in factory.get_provider; provider.py:168/277/359 call get_valid_token once then reuse the returned token), the caller therefore gets a freshly-refreshed VALID token regardless of which row was written. Also, because factory picks the NEWEST-expiry row, the refresh only triggers when even the newest account is near expiry, so the early "already fresh" returns can't mask a fresh row here. No guaranteed 401-loop/lockout. Net: real consistency/correctness defect (esp. the missing is_active filter and wrong-row writes) worth fixing per the recommendation, but realistic blast radius is medium, not high.

confirmed.title: Async client never retries 5xx and applies 429 backoff without jitter or Retry-After
confirmed.description: GBPAsyncClient.request only retries HTTP 429 and httpx network errors. Any 5xx (500/502/503/504) — which Google's Business APIs return transiently with some regularity — falls into `if response.status_code >= 400: raise map_google_error(...)` and is raised immediately with zero retries, so transient Google outages surface as hard task failures. Additionally the 429 backoff is pure exponential with no jitter (`delay = base_delay * (2 ** attempt)`), causing thundering-herd retries across the 10 worker threads, and it ignores the `Retry-After` header that map_google_error already parses into ProviderRateLimitError.retry_after.
confirmed.evidence: client.py:35 `delay = base_delay * (2 ** attempt)` (no jitter); client.py:40-41 `if response.status_code >= 400:\n    raise map_google_error(response.status_code, response.text, response.headers)` — 5xx is raised without retry.
confirmed.recommendation: Treat 5xx (and optionally 408) the same as 429: retry with capped exponential backoff plus random jitter (mirror the jittered backoff already implemented in auth.py:_call_google_refresh_with_retry). When the response carries Retry-After, honor that value for the sleep instead of the computed delay.

The publish Celery task's error classifier (tasks.py:858-869) marks an error retryable ONLY for PermanentAuthError(false), httpx.HTTPStatusError(false), or httpx.RequestError/TimeoutError/ConnectionError; a ProviderTemporaryError (a ProviderError subclass, none of those) falls into line 867-869 `not isinstance(...) -> is_retryable = False`, so a transient Google 5xx becomes a hard FAILED publish job with no retry. confirmed.title: Sentiment tagging has no cost control and a self-amplifying retry/fan-out topology

confirmed.description: The worker runs --pool=threads (process never recycles) and worker.py sets no worker_max_tasks_per_child / worker_max_memory_per_child. optimize_media_task and generate_thumbnail_task load full-resolution images into memory with Pillow (Image.open(io.BytesIO(file_bytes)), resize, save) inside the long-lived worker process. Pillow/native allocations and any per-task leaks accumulate for the life of the container (restart: always only recovers after OOM). With concurrency=10 threads decoding large images simultaneously, peak RSS is 10x a single image's working set and is never reclaimed by child recycling (threads pool can't recycle per-child anyway).
confirmed.evidence: command: celery ... --pool=threads --concurrency=10 (docker-compose.yml:82); worker.py celery.conf.update has no worker_max_tasks_per_child / worker_max_memory_per_child. _optimize_media_async: 'image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(file_bytes)); ... image.save(out_buf, ...)'.
confirmed.recommendation: Run CPU/memory-heavy media tasks on a separate prefork worker with worker_max_tasks_per_child / worker_max_memory_per_child set so the process recycles, or bound concurrency for that queue. Explicitly close PIL images (image.close()) and free buffers. Set a container memory limit so a leak fails loudly rather than swapping.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified all cited facts. worker.py (lines 13-35) celery.conf.update sets NO worker_max_tasks_per_child or worker_max_memory_per_child. docker-compose.yml:82 runs `celery -A app.worker.celery worker --pool=threads --concurrency=10`. The celery_worker service has `restart: always` and NO mem_limit / deploy.resources cap. Both _optimize_media_async (tasks.py:1559) and _generate_thumbnail_async (tasks.py:1657) do `Image.open(io.BytesIO(file_bytes))`, resize/thumbnail with LANCZOS, then `image.save(out_buf, ...)` — neither calls image.close() nor frees file_bytes/out_buf, and there is no Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS guard. Tasks are dispatched via celery_app.send_task on every upload (media.py:65-66). The core mechanism is real: with --pool=threads there is ONE long-lived process shared by 10 threads, so per-child recycling is physically impossible (the worker_max_* settings the auditor wants only apply to the prefork pool — adding them would be a no-op here, which actually strengthens the case that a separate prefork queue is the only fix). Native Pillow/zlib allocations and glibc heap arenas commonly are NOT returned to the OS after free, so RSS ratchets to a high-water mark and stays there for the container's life. HOWEVER the finding OVERSTATES impact in two ways the auditor missed: (1) Input is hard-capped at 10MB BEFORE dispatch (media.py:32-38 reads MAX_SIZE+1 and rejects >10MB with 413), so each task's working set is bounded — not the implied 'multi-GB'. (2) The 'per-task leaks accumulate' claim is largely unsubstantiated: the PIL image and BytesIO buffers are local variables with no persistent references (no module cache, no list append), so CPython garbage-collects them when the coroutine returns. The real effect is a bounded RSS PLATEAU (driven by up-to-10 concurrent decode peaks plus allocator retention), not unbounded growth. There is no max-dimension / MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS check, so a single highly-compressed ~10MB image can transiently decode to a few hundred MB of RGB (decompression-bomb-ish), which is the most legitimate concern and argues for adding Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS plus a container mem_limit. Net: genuine hardening gap, but for an internal MVP with a 10MB upload cap and transient (not accumulating) buffers, medium overstates it — adjusted to low. Recommendation is sound: route media tasks to a separate prefork worker with recycling, add image.close()/explicit frees, add Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, and set a container memory limit.

confirmed.title: sync_locations_task deletes an arbitrary admin's OAuth account on PermanentAuthError (.first(), unordered)

If the organization has multiple admins who each connected Google, this may delete a DIFFERENT admin's still-valid OAuth account rather than the one whose token actually got revoked (ProviderFactory chooses its own credential independently). That can knock out a working connection and force unnecessary re-auth, or leave the actually-revoked account in place.

confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against the actual code. In backend/app/tasks.py:407-411 the PermanentAuthError handler selects the OAuth account to delete with db.query(OAuthAccount).join(User).filter(org_id, role.in_(ADMIN_ROLES), provider.in_(['gbp','google'])).first() — no order_by, so it deletes an arbitrary admin's account. This does NOT match how the credential that actually failed was chosen:

- ProviderFactory.get_provider (backend/app/providers/factory.py:39-50) picks the account deterministically via .order_by(OAuthAccount.expires_at.desc(), User.id.asc()).first() — the freshest token.
- The refresh that raises PermanentAuthError (backend/app/providers/gbp/auth.py:67-71, 117-121, 184-188) selects/refreshes the account with unordered .first() too, and the refresh_token it tests comes from that unordered pick.

The query IS correctly scoped to organization_id, so there is no cross-tenant/IDOR concern — purely a correctness/operational bug. Severity low is appropriate: real and reproducible, but only under the narrow multi-connected-admin condition, with no security/isolation impact, and it occurs only when a token is already genuinely revoked (re-auth already needed for at least one account).

confirmed.title: Module-level caches shared across thread pool are mutated with non-atomic / KeyError-prone patterns
confirmed.description: Celery runs `--pool=threads --concurrency=10` (docker-compose.yml:82), so `_account_id_cache` (provider.py:23) and `_warned_metrics` (provider.py:27) are shared mutable globals across 10 threads each running asyncio.run. Two threads can both read the same expired entry and both attempt `del`; the second raises KeyError, crashing the whole get_reviews/create_post/insights call. _warned_metrics.add (line 592) is comparatively benign but is also unsynchronized.

provider.py:101-103 `if time.time() - resolved_at < _ACCOUNT_ID_CACHE_TTL:
    return account_name
else:
    del _account_id_cache[google_location_id]` — TOCTOU between get and del under concurrent threads.
confirmed.recommendation: Replace the check-then-del with `_account_id_cache.pop(google_location_id, None)` (atomic, no KeyError), or guard all cache mutations with a threading.Lock. Storing TTL in the tuple and only ever using pop/get avoids the race entirely.

Two threads resolving the same google_location_id just past the 3600s TTL can both read the same stale entry via .get(), both enter the else branch, and both attempt `del`; the second raises an uncaught KeyError that propagates out of _resolve_account_id and aborts the calling op (called at lines 308, 372, 418, 799, 838, 875, 909 — get_reviews/create_post/insights). The _warned_metrics.add(line 592) point is correctly flagged as benign — set.add never raises on a duplicate, worst case is a redundant warning log.

Adjusted to low rather than medium: the crash is real but the trigger window is very narrow (same location resolved concurrently on two threads, entry exactly past TTL, both inside the get→del gap). The blast radius is a single aborted/retried task throwing KeyError — no data corruption, no cross-tenant leak, no persistent state damage. Genuine unsynchronized-shared-state bug worth the one-line pop() fix, but practical severity is low.

This is an ops/availability HARDENING gap (the finding's own CATEGORY is 'improvement'), not a code-correctness or security defect. `restart: always` already recovers the common failure mode — an actual process crash/exit. The uncovered case is narrower: a process that stays alive but is internally hung (wedged consumer, stalled beat, broken Redis socket). confirmed.title: os.chmod on static uploads dir at import time will crash on non-POSIX hosts and is futile under bind mount
confirmed.description: At module import the app does os.makedirs + os.chmod(static_uploads_path, S_IRWXU|S_IRGRP|S_IXGRP). os.chmod with POSIX mode bits is meaningful only on POSIX; on Windows it is a near no-op, and more importantly executing filesystem mutations at import time couples app startup to a writable filesystem at a fixed relative path. Under the compose bind mount (./backend:/app) the directory is host-owned, so the chmod result depends on host state and the appuser may lack permission to chmod it, raising PermissionError and crashing startup. This also tightly couples the API process to local-disk storage even when STORAGE_PROVIDER is s3/r2.
confirmed.evidence: main.py:73-74  `os.makedirs(static_uploads_path, exist_ok=True)\nos.chmod(static_uploads_path, stat.S_IRWXU | stat.S_IRGRP | stat.S_IXGRP)` executed at module top level.
confirmed.recommendation: Only create/mount the static dir when STORAGE_PROVIDER=='local'. Wrap the chmod in a try/except (or drop it) and move filesystem setup into the startup event rather than import time, so an unwritable/host-owned mount degrades gracefully instead of crashing the worker/web process.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against the actual code. backend/app/main.py:70-75 does run os.makedirs(static_uploads_path, exist_ok=True) followed by os.chmod(static_uploads_path, stat.S_IRWXU|stat.S_IRGRP|stat.S_IXGRP) at module top level (import time), unconditionally — there is no STORAGE_PROVIDER guard. config.py:86 confirms STORAGE_PROVIDER defaults to "local" but also supports "s3"/"r2", and the local provider (storage/providers/local.py) is the only one that uses this path, so the coupling claim is correct: the dir creation + chmod + /static/uploads mount run even on cloud-storage deployments where they serve nothing. That part of the finding is REAL.

The crash claims are partly overstated, however:
1) "Will crash on non-POSIX hosts (Windows)" is wrong — os.chmod on a directory the process owns does NOT raise on Windows; it is a near no-op (only the read-only attribute is honored, and these bits keep owner-write set). In production this runs in a Linux container anyway.
2) The PermissionError-under-bind-mount path is real but CONDITIONAL, not a guaranteed crash. docker-compose.yml mounts ./backend:/app (lines 44, 84, 113) and backend/Dockerfile (18-22) runs as non-root appuser uid 10001. POSIX chmod requires owner-or-root, so if static/uploads pre-exists on the host owned by a different uid, appuser's chmod raises PermissionError and crashes import. But .gitignore excludes backend/app/static/uploads/, so the dir usually does not pre-exist; makedirs then creates it as appuser, who then owns it and can chmod it successfully. Docker Desktop (Mac/Win) UID remapping also often masks this. So failure is real but not reliable.
3) "Crashes the worker/web process" overstates scope: only the uvicorn web process imports app.main. The celery worker/beat run app.worker.celery + autodiscover app.tasks; worker.py does not import app.main and tasks.py has no app.main/StaticFiles reference (grep returned no matches), so workers are unaffected.

Net: a genuine but minor fragility/code-quality issue — unguarded import-time filesystem mutation with a futile/risky chmod and an unconditional local-storage mount. The recommendation (guard by STORAGE_PROVIDER=='local', wrap chmod in try/except or drop it, move to startup event) is valid. Claimed severity "low" is correct and if anything slightly generous given the conditional nature.

confirmed.title: Razorpay script-load failure throws into an unawaited promise; user sees no error
confirmed.description: openRazorpay is designed to throw when the checkout.js script fails to load ('Throw so the caller's try/catch surfaces a toast'). But every caller invokes openRazorpay(options) WITHOUT await, so the rejected promise escapes the surrounding try/catch (the synchronous part already completed) and becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The intended error toast never fires. Net effect: on a flaky connection / blocked CDN, the user clicks Pay, an order is created and charged-nothing, and the UI silently does nothing.

Verified the hook and all four call sites. In frontend/hooks/useRazorpay.ts, openRazorpay is declared `async` (line 45). loadScript's script.onerror calls resolve(false) (lines 38-40), so on script-load failure openRazorpay throws at line 50 — which, because the function is async, becomes a REJECTED PROMISE rather than a synchronous throw.

All four callers invoke it WITHOUT await:
- TopUpModal.tsx:62 `openRazorpay(options as any);`
- UpgradeModal.tsx:157 (handleUpgrade) and :63 (handleUnlock)
- RemandateBanner.tsx:37 (handleApprove)

When the script load later fails, the rejection fires outside the try/catch scope -> unhandled promise rejection, and the intended toast.error never runs.
