The cited useEffect matches the evidence exactly: setInterval(refetch, 3000) is created whenever (subscription_status==='trial' && !trial_ends_at) || is_org_locked. The only cleanup is clearInterval on effect re-run/unmount. There is genuinely no attempt cap, no backoff, and no max duration, so if a webhook never reconciles or the org stays permanently locked, the page polls /billing/status every 3s indefinitely while the tab is open. The underlying useBillingStatus hook (hooks/useBilling.ts) is a plain react-query GET with no refetchInterval, so the setInterval is the sole driver — the unbounded-poll claim is accurate. The second half of the finding (billing:refresh is dead code) is partly a misread: I grepped the codebase and the event IS dispatched by UpgradeModal.tsx (lines 89, 143) and RemandateBanner.tsx (line 58) and IS consumed by DashboardClient.tsx (lines 285-289), where it imperatively reloads the locations grid that isn't in the react-query cache (per the inline comment). So the event is not globally dead — it has an intentional, documented consumer. It is true the billing page itself does not listen for it and instead relies on invalidateQueries(['billing_status']) (which the modals/TopUpModal also call), but these are complementary mechanisms (query cache vs non-cached grid), not redundant parallel ones, so the recommendation to remove the dispatches is wrong. Net: the unbounded-poll defect is real but low impact — a handful of extra authenticated GETs/min on an already-rendered settings page, only in transient/locked states, only while the tab is open; no security, correctness, or data-integrity consequence. Low severity stands.

rejected.title: Float arithmetic in annual price and proration relies on round()/int() truncation rather than integer paise math
rejected.whyRejected: Verified pricing_service.py:39-42 and 61-77 plus plan_config.py. The code does use float math: line 41 `int(annual * (1 - plan_config.ANNUAL_DISCOUNT))` with ANNUAL_DISCOUNT=0.20 (plan_config.py:20), and line 77 `round(marginal * days_left / days_in_cycle)`. However, the claimed defect (rounding drift / systematic undercharge) does NOT actually occur with the current config. I exhaustively tested all location counts 1..500 (the full MIN/MAX_LOCATIONS range): the float annual computation equals exact integer paise math (annual*80//100) in 100% of cases — zero mismatches, zero undercharge. The finding itself concedes "with 0.20 the float is exact." Two further inaccuracies in the claim: (a) proration uses round() (nearest), not int()/truncation, so the "always rounds DOWN" characterization applies only to the annual line, not proration; (b) proration is clamped to [0, marginal] (line 77) and the add-on amount is floored at _MIN_ORDER_PAISE (subscription_service.py:301), so any theoretical 1-paise drift is bounded and economically negligible. Money is otherwise kept in integer paise; price tiers are multiples of 50,000 paise (plan_config.py:12-16). The only substance is a hypothetical "a future discount like 0.15/0.333 could introduce representation error" — that is forward-looking code hygiene, not a present, reproducible bug. Since there is no current mis-charge, isReal=false. The refactor to explicit integer-percent math is a reasonable defensive improvement but does not fix any existing defect; severity stays low if treated as a hardening suggestion.

rejected.title: run_async = asyncio.run() per call: a fresh event loop is created/destroyed for every async hop inside a single task
rejected.whyRejected:
I verified each cited fact and the underlying mechanism.

CONFIRMED FACTS: tasks.py line 20-25 is exactly `def run_async(coro): return asyncio.run(coro)`. asyncio.run() does create and tear down a fresh event loop per call. Tasks do call run_async multiple times in sequence: publish_location_media_task calls run_async(provider.create_location_media(...)) at 2044 then run_async(provider.list_location_media(...)) at 2066; publish_location_attributes_task calls run_async(_do_publish(...)) at 3031 then run_async(provider.get_location_attributes(...)) at 3066. So the literal "asyncio.run per call, multiple per task" observation is accurate.

WHY THE FINDING IS NOT REAL AS DESCRIBED: The finding's load-bearing claim is that the per-call event loop is what prevents httpx connection-pool/TCP/TLS reuse across hops within a task, and that consolidating to a single asyncio.run wrapping one AsyncClient would fix it. That misdiagnoses the code. I read backend/app/providers/gbp/client.py: GBPAsyncClient.__aenter__ creates a brand-new httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30.0) and __aexit__ calls aclose(). Every GBPProvider method (provider.py lines 113,199,307,371,424,456,553,695,752,766,808,844,879,931 — confirmed via grep) wraps its work in `async with GBPAsyncClient(...)`, i.e. it instantiates and destroys its own AsyncClient + connection pool per method invocation. BaseProvider (base/provider.py) is abstract/stateless and holds no persistent client. Therefore the connection pool is created and torn down per provider-method-call independently of the event loop; even if all hops ran under one shared loop, no TCP/TLS connection would be reused because the client lifetime is scoped inside each method, not the task. The recommended fix (single asyncio.run reusing one AsyncClient) would NOT yield connection reuse without also refactoring GBPAsyncClient/provider to accept and reuse an injected client — which the finding does not call out.

RESIDUAL TRUTH AND SEVERITY: There is a genuine but minor cost in recreating the event loop per call (loop setup/teardown is microsecond-to-low-millisecond, well under the network latency of a TLS handshake to Google), and the real connection-reuse loss lives in the provider/client layer, not in run_async. The stated mechanism and remedy are wrong, so I mark isReal=false. If counted purely as "asyncio.run loop churn," severity would still be low/negligible, so the claimed low severity is not understated.

rejected.title: sync_all_insights_beat_task / archive / cleanup load whole tables with .all() — unbounded memory as data grows
rejected.whyRejected:
I read tasks.py around all three cited locations and the beat schedule in worker.py. The literal `.all()` calls exist, but the finding as described is largely a misread and not a reproducible issue.

1) sync_all_insights_beat_task (line 2510): `db.query(Organization).all()` is real and over-fetches full ORM rows when only org.id is used. But Organizations == tenant count, which is inherently bounded/small in a multi-tenant SaaS. Runs DAILY at 1AM (worker.py line 63-66), not "nightly+hourly". Trivial footprint.

2) retry_failed_sentiment_beat_task (line 2546): the description claims it does a "DISTINCT (location_id, organization_id) over the entire reviews table" and "holds the entire table in memory." This misreads the code. It selects only 2 columns (tuples, not ORM objects) AND filters `Review.sentiment_tagged_at == None` AND `is_deleted == False`. The DISTINCT is computed server-side by Postgres; Python only materializes distinct UNTAGGED (location, org) pairs. Since tagging is event-driven and this task only catches the failure/miss backlog, the result set is near-empty in steady state — it is NOT the whole reviews table. Hourly cadence (worker.py line 67-71) is fine because the query is selective.

3) sync_all_active_categories_metadata_task (line 2587): selects 2 columns with `.distinct()`; distinct (category_resource_name, org) pairs is bounded by the number of GBP categories (small). It is also not present in the active beat_schedule in worker.py, so it runs manually/rarely, not on a hot loop.

4) The finding title also claims "archive / cleanup load whole tables with .all()". This is FALSE: archive_old_activity_logs_task (lines 2174-2234) is explicitly paginated with batch_size=500 via `.limit(batch_size).all()` in a `while True` loop with per-batch commit — exactly the recommended pattern. cleanup_deleted_media_task delegates to async with no table-wide .all().

Net: the only genuinely unbounded-by-nothing-else query is Organization.all(), which is bounded by tenant count and merely over-fetches columns — a trivial nit. The two "unbounded as data grows" candidates the finding leans on are either a bounded tenant table or a selectively-filtered, server-side-distinct, 2-column near-empty result. The described mechanism (DISTINCT over entire reviews table held in memory; archive loading whole tables) does not match the code and is not reproducible at realistic scale, so isReal=false; if anything it is a low-severity micro-optimization at most.

rejected.title: Account-ID cache keyed only by google_location_id, not organization — cross-tenant resolution risk
rejected.whyRejected:
I read backend/app/providers/gbp/provider.py (lines 1-200, 295-434), backend/app/providers/gbp/auth.py (full), backend/app/providers/base/auth.py, and the Location model. The finding misreads the threat model.

The cache `_account_id_cache: Dict[str, tuple]` (line 23) is keyed on google_location_id and stores (account_name, timestamp). The cited evidence is accurate that there is no organization_id in the key. However, this does NOT create a cross-tenant resolution risk for these reasons:

1) The cached value is org-INVARIANT by Google's data model. google_location_id (e.g. "locations/12345") is a Google-global identifier; a given Google location object belongs to exactly one Google account (account_name, e.g. "accounts/67890"). Org A and org B both resolving the same google_location_id will deterministically resolve to the SAME account_name. The resolved value is not derived from org A's private state — it is a function of the location id alone. So serving org A's cached account_name to org B yields the identical value org B would have resolved itself.

2) account_name is NOT a credential and confers no access. At every call site (lines 308, 372, 418, 799, 838, 875, 909) the cached account_name is only used to build a URL path like .../v4/{account_name}/{google_location_id}/.... Every actual HTTP request is authenticated with the REQUESTING org's own OAuth token from self._auth.get_valid_token(). That token is strictly org-scoped: GBPAuthManager fetches the OAuthAccount via a User.organization_id == auth_context.organization_id join (auth.py lines 67-71, 117-121, 184-188). Google enforces authorization server-side against that token — if org B's token lacks access to accounts/67890/locations/12345, Google returns 403/404. A path-only account_name grants nothing.

3) Even a stale/poisoned cache entry cannot cause a confidentiality breach. A wrong account_name would simply produce a failed (404/403) Google call until the 3600s TTL expires — an availability/correctness annoyance, not cross-tenant data exposure. No token, payment secret, or tenant data is held in this cache.

For two orgs to even share a cache entry, both would have to store the identical google_location_id in their Location rows; in the normal one-location-one-tenant model this doesn't happen, and even if it did the shared value is the same public Google resource name.

The DB back-fill at lines 105-108 is correctly org-scoped, but that is the DB path, not the cache. The recommendation to key on (organization_id, google_location_id) is a harmless defense-in-depth/robustness improvement, but the claimed IDOR/cross-tenant-leak and the "medium security" severity overstate impact. Downgrading to low and marking not real as a security vulnerability — the only genuine (minor) residual is a robustness nit around stale entries if a location migrates between Google accounts.

rejected.title: Token-exchange JSON parsing raises raw KeyError on missing fields
rejected.whyRejected: The literal code observation is accurate: both backend/app/providers/gbp/provider.py (lines 75, 82, 84) and backend/app/core/gbp_client.py (lines 95, 102, 104) use bracket indexing tokens['access_token'] / tokens['expires_in'] without .get or validation, so a 200 response with a body missing those keys would raise KeyError. The claimed line numbers and the duplicate pattern in gbp_client.py are both confirmed. However, the finding's STATED IMPACT is wrong, which is the crux of the claim. (1) A non-200 / OAuth-error response cannot reach the indexing: provider.py:68-69 and gbp_client.py:88-89 do `if response.status_code != 200: raise Exception(...)` first, so an error-shaped OAuth body with a non-200 status never hits the bracket access. Only a 200-with-malformed-body — rare for Google's token endpoint — can trigger the KeyError. (2) The claim that the KeyError 'surfaces as a generic 500 to the OAuth callback rather than a clear auth failure' is false. The callback in backend/app/api/auth.py wraps the whole flow (including ProviderFactory.exchange_code_for_tokens at line 78) in try/except. The catch-all `except Exception` at lines 409-412 rolls back the DB, logs, and returns RedirectResponse to {FRONTEND_URL}/login?error=oauth_failed. So a KeyError produces a clean login-page redirect with an error flag, not a 500 — which is already the 'clear auth error to the OAuth callback' the recommendation requests. The issue is therefore already mitigated by surrounding error handling; the only residual is cosmetic (generic oauth_failed vs. a token-shape-specific message and a noisier traceback in logs). Given the impact is already neutralized and the trigger is a rare edge case, this is not a genuine actionable issue as described — isReal=false; if anything it is a code-quality nicety at most.

rejected.title: Insight sync issues one unbounded multi-row INSERT for the full date range (no chunking)
rejected.whyRejected:
The code facts in the finding are accurate: insight_sync_service.py:171-198 builds one insert_values list for the whole [start_date, end_date] range and executes a single insert().values().on_conflict_do_update() with no chunking, whereas review_sync_service.py:154-156 explicitly chunks at 500. So the asymmetry is real. However, the claimed RISK (parameter-limit / memory fragility on large backfills) is not reproducible in this codebase, so I mark isReal=false.

I traced every enqueue site of the task via grep over app/: there are exactly two callers that ever produce a date range. (1) The nightly beat task sync_all_insights_beat_task (tasks.py:2511-2520) uses today-7 .. yesterday = ~7 rows. (2) The manual/on-load API endpoint (insights.py:838-847) hardcodes a 90-day window (yesterday-90 .. yesterday) = ~91 rows. The org-level fan-out (sync_organization_insights_task) just forwards those same start/end strings unchanged to per-location sync. There is NO 18-month / 540-row backfill entry point anywhere in the repo; the finding's worst case is hypothetical.

Parameter math: the val dict has 24 columns/row. Worst realistic case 91 rows = 2,184 bind params; even the hypothetical 540 rows = 12,960 params. PostgreSQL's protocol limit is 65,535 params/statement (sync psycopg2 engine confirmed in db/session.py). You'd need ~2,730 rows (~7.5 yrs in a single location call) to hit the limit, which no caller can generate. Additionally, for non-Manual runs the task clamps start_date to the first day of the previous month (tasks.py:2274-2282), further bounding the window.

Conclusion: this is a legitimate code-consistency/style observation (two sync paths batch differently) but not a genuine, reproducible performance or memory hazard given the actual call sites. Functionally correct for all real ranges. Informational at most; the claimed 'low' severity already over-states real impact, so I leave adjustedSeverity=low as the floor of the scale.

rejected.title: docker-compose runs uvicorn with --reload and a source-bind-mount as the 'always restart' deployment
rejected.whyRejected:
I read docker-compose.yml in full, backend/Dockerfile in full, PROJECT_OVERVIEW.md, and .env.example, and globbed for any other compose files.

The finding's literal observations are accurate: docker-compose.yml:42 is exactly `command: sh -c "alembic upgrade head && uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload"`, lines 43-44 bind-mount `./backend:/app`, line 41 is `restart: always`, and Dockerfile:18-22 do create/chown a non-root appuser that the bind mount would overlay. There is indeed only one docker-compose.yml and one backend Dockerfile (the other matches are all in frontend/node_modules), and no override/prod compose exists.

However, the finding's load-bearing premise — that this single file IS the production "deployment artifact" — misreads the repo. The intent is documented unambiguously as LOCAL DEVELOPMENT: PROJECT_OVERVIEW.md:103 labels it `docker-compose.yml  # Local development infrastructure`; the setup instructions live under a heading literally named "Local Development Setup" (lines 214-215); line 238 notes "Development frontend and backend run on different ports". Every concrete value confirms dev-only intent: compose hardcodes `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: http://localhost:8000/api/v1` (line 140/148), and .env.example uses localhost redirect URIs, a JWT_SECRET literally suffixed `changeinproduction`, and a publicly-known placeholder ENCRYPTION_KEY. PROJECT_OVERVIEW:308 also confirms there is no CI/CD or deployment pipeline ("No .github/workflows found"). 

For a local dev compose, `--reload` + source bind mount is the correct, intended pattern (live code reload is the whole point), and `restart: always` is cosmetic convenience, not evidence of a production deployment. The Dockerfile-chown-vs-bind-mount observation is irrelevant on a single-developer local host. So this is not a genuine production security vulnerability; it is at most a hygiene/best-practice suggestion to add a dedicated prod compose/profile (with `--workers`/gunicorn, no `--reload`, no bind mount) before this is ever deployed. That makes the high-severity security framing incorrect. Marking isReal=false because the central claim (production deployment artifact running --reload) does not match the code's documented purpose; the residual value is a low-severity readiness note.

rejected.title: Backend error message reflected into login URL and rendered to user
rejected.whyRejected:
I read all four relevant files. The SINK the finding describes literally exists: LoginSuccessClient.tsx:38 does `router.replace(\`/login?error=profile_fetch_failed&details=${encodeURIComponent(errorMsg)}\`)`, and LoginClient.tsx:30-34 reads `details` and interpolates it into `friendlyMessage`, rendered at lines 78-82 as React children (auto-escaped — so the finding's "no HTML injection, low severity" reasoning is sound). lib/api.ts:121-141 confirms backend `detail` strings/arrays/objects (incl. `JSON.stringify(errorData.detail)`) flow into the thrown Error's `.message`, exactly as claimed.

However, the finding is NOT reproducible because the catch block that builds the `details=` URL is effectively dead code for the described "failed profile fetch" path. In LoginSuccessClient.tsx the only awaited call in the try block (line 24) is `refresh()`. `refresh` is destructured from `useAuth()` (line 12), and useAuth.tsx:67 maps `refresh: fetchProfile`. `fetchProfile` (useAuth.tsx:28-37) wraps `api.get('/users/me')` in its OWN try/catch that swallows the error, sets `user=null`, and returns void — it never re-throws. So a failed profile fetch resolves `refresh()` successfully; control proceeds to the success `setTimeout` and redirects to `/dashboard`, never to the `error=profile_fetch_failed&details=...` URL. The catch in LoginSuccessClient.tsx:35-39 can only fire on an unrelated synchronous throw (e.g. from router/state), which would not carry a backend error body. Thus the specific exploit chain ("backend error message reflected into login URL and rendered") cannot actually occur as described. The code that would propagate the raw message is unreachable from the cited trigger, so the finding misreads the control flow. Severity is academic, but if it were reachable, low is the correct rating (same-origin, React-escaped, self-inflicted only).

rejected.title: Billing poll effect churns its interval via object-identity deps
rejected.whyRejected:
Read frontend/app/dashboard/settings/billing/page.tsx (effect at lines 241-251), the useBilling hook (frontend/hooks/useBilling.ts: useBillingStatus is a plain useQuery returning data/refetch), and the QueryClient config (frontend/components/QueryProvider.tsx). The finding's premise — "each refetch makes a new billing ref, recreating the interval every cycle" — is false because of two TanStack Query v5 (package.json: ^5.100.14) guarantees:

1) `refetch` from useQuery is a stable, memoized callback; it does NOT change identity when data changes, so it is not a churn source.

2) `billing` is `data`, and structuralSharing defaults to true (not overridden in QueryProvider's defaultOptions). While in the locked / pending-activation state, the /billing/status response is deeply equal on every 3s poll (still is_org_locked:true or trial with no trial_ends_at), so structural sharing returns the SAME object reference. The dependency array [billing, refetch] therefore does not change, the effect does NOT re-run, and the single interval is created once — not recreated every cycle.

Even in the impossible-here hypothetical that the ref changed each poll, the effect has a correct cleanup (return () => clearInterval(interval)), so the old interval is cleared before a new one is created — no stacked intervals, no leak, and the cadence stays 3s. Polling correctly STOPS when the webhook resolves the state: the response payload changes, billing's ref changes, the effect re-runs, the condition is false, the old interval is cleaned up and no new one is created. "Polls forever while locked" is the intended behavior (poll until webhook fixes activation). No functional defect; the finding misreads React Query's structural-sharing and stable-refetch semantics. Severity lowered to low (at most a cosmetic/style nit; recommendation to use refetchInterval is stylistic, not a bug fix).

rejected.title: Campaign polling effect omits `campaigns` from deps, can poll a terminal campaign forever
rejected.whyRejected: Read frontend/app/dashboard/posts/page.tsx lines 261-333 (the polling effect, loadCampaignProgress) and traced every setter of selectedCampaignId/pollNonce (lines 225,239,253,319,448,449,532). The finding misreads the control flow on two points. (1) "Polling continues indefinitely against a campaign that already completed" after a transient failure is false: the interval at lines 292-298 re-fetches on EVERY 3s tick via loadCampaignProgress(); a transient failure returns undefined only for that single tick, and the next tick does a fresh fetch that returns the terminal status and calls clearInterval. So a transient failure delays detection by 3s, it does not make polling permanent. "Indefinitely" only holds if every future fetch fails forever (backend permanently down), which is not a stale-deps bug and self-corrects the moment the backend recovers — and a 3s retry loop in that degenerate state is harmless/arguably correct. (2) The stale-campaigns claim is misdirected: the line-287 guard (campaigns.find / isTerminal(current?.status)) is purely an initial-mount optimization to avoid starting an interval when the cached snapshot is already terminal. Ongoing terminal detection inside the interval does NOT read the stale campaigns snapshot at all — it uses the live `updated` value returned by each fetch (line 294). So "the guard at line 287 never re-evaluates" is true but irrelevant; it doesn't need to. Even the reverse stale case (snapshot shows non-terminal while campaign is actually terminal) self-resolves: line 285's immediate fetch plus the first interval tick stop it within ~3s. The deps [selectedCampaignId, pollNonce] are sufficient because every campaign selection/creation/retry bumps pollNonce or changes selectedCampaignId, re-running the effect with a fresh snapshot. Net: no genuine reproducible bug. At most there is a minor cosmetic issue of one extra poll cycle; severity lowered to low. The recommendation (bail after N consecutive failed polls) is a hardening nicety, not a fix for a real defect.

rejected.title: Relative-time helpers parse timezone-naive timestamps as local, yielding negative/"future" durations
rejected.whyRejected:
The frontend helpers exist exactly as quoted (ActivityTab.tsx:6-21 formatDistanceToNow; posts/page.tsx:76-85 relativeTime; DashboardClient.tsx:571-580 relativeTime; reviews/page.tsx:220-237 renderSlaBadge), and none clamp diffMs to >=0. So the code shape matches. HOWEVER, the finding's core premise — that the API serializes timestamps WITHOUT a timezone suffix, making new Date() interpret them as local — is false for this codebase, which is what drives the alleged bug.

I verified the backend serialization path end to end: (1) Every timestamp column feeding these helpers is declared DateTime(timezone=True) i.e. PostgreSQL timestamptz — activity_log.created_at (models/activity_log.py:44-46), review.review_created_at / reply_created_at / created_at (models/review.py:20-24), location.last_synced_at (models/location.py:32), sync_log.created_at, post.created_at, campaign.created_at. (2) The driver is psycopg2-binary (requirements.txt) with SQLAlchemy 2.0; for timestamptz, psycopg2 returns timezone-AWARE Python datetimes. (3) db/session.py creates the engine with no connect_args / timezone override. (4) The response schemas (schemas/listing_edits.py ActivityLogResponse.created_at:53, schemas/review.py ReviewResponse:17-20) type these as plain datetime with from_attributes=True and NO json_encoders / field_serializer / validator that would strip tzinfo (grep for json_encoders|field_serializer|model_serializer|astimezone|replace(tzinfo across schemas returned nothing). (5) Pydantic is v2 (>=2.9.0), which serializes tz-aware datetimes to ISO-8601 WITH an explicit offset (e.g. '2026-06-14T10:00:00+00:00'). (6) The review sync service writes tz-aware UTC values (review_sync_service.py uses datetime.now(timezone.utc) throughout), so even ingested review timestamps are aware.

I confirmed the JS impact empirically with node under TZ=America/New_York: parsing the AWARE string the backend actually emits ('...+00:00') yields the correct ~0-minute diff, whereas the NAIVE string the finding assumes would yield -240 minutes. Since the backend emits the offset, the negative/'future' duration described does not occur in normal operation. The only residual is harmless sub-minute clock skew rendering 'just now', and the lack of a diffMs>=0 clamp is at most a trivial defensive-coding nit, not a medium bug. Hence isReal=false; severity downgraded to low.

rejected.title: Keyword & leaderboard rows keyed by array index across sorting/pagination
rejected.whyRejected:
I read both cited files in full at the relevant sections.

KEYWORD TABLE (search-intelligence/page.tsx:479-480): The auditor's core premise is factually wrong. Sorting and pagination are NOT client-side — they are server-side. fetchKeywords (lines 68-82) sends sort_by/sort_desc/page/page_size to the API and replaces the entire array with setKeywords(res?.items ?? []). When sort or page changes, useEffect re-runs fetchKeywords and React reconciles a brand-new array; there is no in-place reorder of a retained array. The rows (481-498) are 100% presentational: they render kw.keyword, kw.impressions.toLocaleString(), a pure <Delta v=...> and a pure <Badge>. No row-local useState, no uncontrolled inputs, no autofocus, no mount-keyed animation (only static CSS hover:bg-muted/20). Index keys are problematic ONLY when rows carry positional state (inputs/focus/animation) that must follow the data; none of that exists here, so the claimed symptoms ("row state/animations and any focus mis-associated", "stale cell content briefly renders against the wrong row") cannot occur — React correctly updates the text content of each <td> every render.

LEADERBOARD (insights/page.tsx:991): Here sortLeaderboard (642-653) IS client-side and returns a re-ordered [...rows].sort() copy, so key={idx} is the genuine anti-pattern. But the rows (992-1014) again hold zero row-local state/inputs/focus/mount-animations — only a <Link> and static text that are pure functions of props. So even with index keys there is no observable mis-association; at worst it's a reconciliation-efficiency / best-practice nit, not a reproducible bug.

MoM COMPARISON TABLES (1047, 1097): The auditor is wrong to include these. They map over a STATIC inline literal array of 6 fixed metric rows that is never sorted or paginated; index keys are perfectly stable and correct here.

Verdict: The factual claim about client-side re-sorting of the keyword table is false; and across all three tables there is no row-local state/focus/uncontrolled-input/animation that index keying could corrupt, so no real, reproducible bug. It is at most a low-severity style preference (prefer stable keys), which is why I set isReal=false and adjusted severity to low.

rejected.title: useBillingStatus() called without auth-ready gating on the dashboard, unlike billing page
rejected.whyRejected:
Checked the hook, both callers, and the auth provider. The finding misreads the code.

useBilling.ts (lines 32-41): `useBillingStatus(enabled = true)` already gates the query with `enabled: !!user && enabled`. The `enabled` param is ANDed with `!!user`, so it is purely additive — `!!user` alone already prevents the request from firing before auth resolves. Whether the caller passes nothing (enabled=true on the dashboard) or `isAuthReady` (billing page), the query cannot fire while `user` is falsy.

useAuth.tsx (lines 24-50): `user` is initialized to `null` via `useState(null)` with no synchronous/localStorage hydration. It only becomes truthy inside `fetchProfile()` AFTER `GET /users/me` succeeds, at which point `loading` is also set to false in the same function. So there is no window where `user` is truthy but auth is unresolved. Consequently `useBillingStatus()` on the dashboard (DashboardClient.tsx line 151) will NOT fire `/billing/status` pre-auth and will NOT produce a spurious 401. The claimed "avoidable early 401" does not occur.

On the billing page (settings/billing/page.tsx lines 226-227, 261), `isAuthReady = !loading` is passed, but its real purpose is driving the page's own loading skeleton (line 261); as a query gate it is largely redundant with the hook's existing `!!user` check. `retry: false` is set on the query (line 39) regardless of caller, so retry behavior is identical too.

The banner at DashboardClient.tsx line 657 renders only when `billing && (billing.pending_location_count ?? 0) > 0`. While `billing` is undefined it simply doesn't render and then appears once data loads — ordinary progressive loading identical to the billing page, not a "flicker" introduced by the missing arg. The argument difference changes neither the request timing nor the render behavior. Mildly inconsistent style at most; no functional bug, so the claim as written (early 401 / flicker) is not real.

rejected.title: Activity log renders raw JSON.stringify of unbounded `details` with no size/empty guard
rejected.whyRejected:
The cited line exists verbatim — ActivityTab.tsx:86 renders `
{JSON.stringify(log.details, null, 2)}
` and the virtualization TODO is on line 28. However, the finding's substantive claims misread the code due to a field-name mismatch the auditor missed. The backend endpoint GET /locations/{id}/activity (backend/app/api/listing_edits.py:239-260) returns `ActivityLogResponse`, whose schema (backend/app/schemas/listing_edits.py:51) serializes the JSONB column as `payload: Optional[dict]` — NOT `details`. The ActivityLog model column is literally named `payload` (backend/app/models/activity_log.py:38). The frontend api client (frontend/lib/api.ts:149) returns raw `response.json()` with zero key transformation, and a frontend grep confirms nothing maps `payload`→`details`. Therefore `log.details` is always `undefined` for every row. Consequences vs. the finding: (1) "renders the string 'null' when null" is false — the value is `undefined`, and `JSON.stringify(undefined,...)` returns the JS value `undefined`, which React renders as empty, not 'null'; (2) "renders a large pretty-printed blob per row / expensive render" never happens because the component reads a key the API never sends, so nothing renders at all; (3) the "not an XSS sink" note is correct (it is auto-escaped JSX text). The finding also overlooked that line 85 already wraps the

There is a genuine but different bug — the activity feed silently shows no payload because of the payload/details key mismatch — but the specific symptoms and mechanism described in FE-UI-8 are not reproducible, so the finding as written is not real. Severity remains low either way (cosmetic, no security/data-integrity impact).

rejected.title: Posts campaign progress bar can divide by zero / overflow when total_locations is 0
rejected.whyRejected:
Verified the cited code and the full data flow. frontend/app/dashboard/posts/page.tsx:468 defines pct = (n,d) => Math.round((n/(d||1))*100), used at line 540 (list bar) and 609 (big progress bar). The finding's premise — that total_published can exceed total_locations (or that total_locations=0 while total_published>0) during polling — does not hold against the backend invariants:

1) total_locations and total_published are derived from the same source atomically. On launch (backend/app/api/posts.py:173-176) campaign.total_locations = len(payload.location_ids) is set while total_published is simultaneously reset to 0, and exactly one publish job is dispatched per location.

2) total_published is incremented strictly per successful job (backend/app/tasks.py:794 'total_published + 1' and the sharded path at :1435 'total_published + shard_success'), with one job per location. There is no code path that increments published beyond the job/location count, so total_published <= total_locations is an enforced invariant. A campaign with total_locations==0 dispatches zero jobs, so total_published can never become >0.

3) For the only realizable zero case (a DRAFT/unlaunched campaign with total_locations==0), total_published is also 0, so pct(0,0) = round((0/1)*100) = 0 — not >100. The d||1 guard correctly prevents NaN/Infinity.

4) Even hypothetically, both bar containers carry overflow-hidden (lines 539 and 608), so any >100% width would be clipped — the claimed visible 'over-full state' would not render as described.

The finding misreads the model by assuming numerator/denominator can drift independently during transient polling snapshots; polling returns a single consistent DB row where published is monotonically bounded by total_locations. Not a genuine, reproducible issue. Adding Math.min(100, ...) would be harmless defensive hardening but is not fixing any real defect.
